articles.title: NASA deliberately crashed into an asteroid. Now scientists are surveying the damage.
articles.description: A spacecraft has arrived at an asteroid to investigate the damage caused by an unprecedented cosmic crash. In what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft deliberately smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it off course. The Nasa craft was obliterated on impact. Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) mission, called Hera, is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision - with the first images set to be released later on Wednesday. The asteroid poses no threat, instead this was the first ever test of our planetary defences to see what action we could take if a space rock was heading for our planet. "Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission. The crash test focussed on a pair of asteroids: a larger one called Didymos - about 730m (2,400ft) wide - which is orbited by a smaller rock called Dimorphos, about 150m (490ft) wide. The Dart spacecraft targeted Dimorphos, hurtling into the rock at 22,000km per hour (14,000mph). Images beamed back showed the asteroid's rocky surface coming ever closer until the feed cut out on impact. It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 10,000km long (6,200 miles), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space. The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid. Before the collision it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the Dart crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes. But the arrival of the second spacecraft, Hera, will help scientists to answer many more questions. "Dart exploded in the asteroid, and therefore we don't have the information of what is its final state," explained Michel. "The impact could have left a crater - and if it is the case, we need to understand the size and the depth. Or [the impact] may have entirely reshaped the asteroid." The Hera mission will spend the next year studying Dimorphos, and take a look at Didymos too. The spacecraft is packed with instruments, and it also has two small shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid. A key task is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was. This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth. "It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team. "We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'." Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet. The biggest, which measure more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city. "We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst, Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who works on both the Dart and Hera missions. "The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there." She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted, and none are heading to Earth. "The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added. "But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are, and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity. And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that." Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks - to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us. A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids: a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor. There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including to one called Apophis, which is about 450m (1,480ft) long. Apophis was discovered in 2004 and it was initially thought it might hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029. But now scientists understand its orbit better, and say it won't hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above our surface. This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close. Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA). articles.title: Lab says humanoid robot uses living human neurons to help think
articles.description: A San Francisco lab is showing off Iris, a humanoid robot with a mood informed by real, living human cells. The lab says the robot communicates wirelessly with lab-grown neurons that originated with human stem cells, which work with complicated AI to help her decide how to feel. It’s an early step for an experiment into how human intelligence can meet artificial intelligence. NBC News’ Steve Patterson reports.

articles.title: test | The US Sun
New chemical route delivers first synthesis of plant compound with cough-suppressing potential
articles.description: Neotuberostemonine, a complex plant-derived alkaloid with promising antitussive activity, has remained a challenging target for chemical synthesis for nearly 30 years. Researchers have now achieved its first total synthesis, alongside the synthesis of neostenine and the putative structure of tuberostemonine L. The findings also reveal how the nearly planar geometry of nitrogen atoms contributes to the oxidative instability of these alkaloids, offering new insights and synthetic strategies for natural-product chemistry and future drug discovery.

articles.description: For decades, computers have steadily grown faster and more powerful. Avik Dutt, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the University of Maryland, envisions another dramatic leap forward—one propelled by the quantum properties of light.

articles.title: Laser light reveals where electrons accumulate in atomically thin semiconductor stacks
articles.description: Stacking semiconductors—the chips that power phones, computers and so much more—enables quicker signal movement with less energy, but how does the process actually work? Turns out shining a literal light on the semiconducting materials can help elucidate how the electrons move in the stack, according to a multi-institutional team in Japan. The approach could help inform the development of more efficient, low-power electronics, the researchers said.

articles.title: Underwater robots reveal first salp species known to live exclusively in deep sea
articles.description: Salps are barrel-shaped gelatinous animals that play an important role in ocean ecosystems. More than 20 years ago, researchers observed an unfamiliar salp in the deep waters of Monterey Bay. Using specimens and data collected by MBARI's advanced underwater robots, Larry Madin, deputy director emeritus at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and an MBARI adjunct, recently published a detailed description of the glass salp (Vitreosalpa gemini) in the journal Marine Biodiversity. This striking species is the first salp known to live exclusively in the deep sea.

articles.title: New workflow advances programmable chromosome editing in plants
articles.description: A study published in Nature Protocols on Nov. 17 presents a detailed experimental workflow for programmable chromosome manipulation in plants. The platform was developed by a research group led by Gao Caixia at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
